interactions: Donepezil + Escitalopram: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction; both can prolong the QT interval (escitalopram dose-dependently), so the combination carries an additive QT risk. Obtain a baseline ECG before starting and repeat it if symptoms such as syncope or palpitations occur.
Donepezil + Ibuprofen (as needed): no pharmacokinetic interaction; cholinesterase inhibitors increase gastric acid secretion, so regular NSAID use adds to the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
warnings: Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia, heart block and syncope; check pulse before starting and after dose increases (heart rate 70 bpm at this visit).
Nausea, diarrhoea, anorexia and vivid dreams are common at initiation; start at 5 mg and increase to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if tolerated.
Avoid adding anticholinergic medicines, which oppose the effect of cholinesterase inhibitors.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic-predominant multi-domain impairment on MoCA and MMSE with little benefit from cueing, informant-confirmed decline over two years, and loss of instrumental independence (unable to work despite reminders)
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive assessment with informant history, a per-domain profile and an explicit account of daily function
action_criteria.rationale: Two clinicians attributed her decline to anxiety; a bedside instrument and her husband's account of the loss of work function establish the syndrome and its stage [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe rapid-forgetting verbal and nonverbal memory impairment with milder naming, fluency and executive deficits, valid effort, and a mood score that does not explain the deficit
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing with an effort measure to characterize the profile and set a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Objective testing with a validity measure separates a neurodegenerative amnestic syndrome from cognitive complaints of anxiety or depression, which is the question two prior clinicians left open [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: All values within normal limits; no metabolic, thyroid, nutritional, or inflammatory mimic identified
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid, B12, folate, syphilis and metabolic causes must be excluded before a neurodegenerative diagnosis, even with a striking family history [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA score 2) atypical for age 51; mild posterior parietal sulcal prominence; no vascular, inflammatory, or neoplastic lesion
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with a volumetric dementia protocol to assess medial temporal atrophy and exclude structural lesions
action_criteria.rationale: At 51, MRI must exclude a structural, vascular or inflammatory cause and shows whether medial temporal atrophy is beyond what age explains [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and at 51 it gives biological support to the diagnosis whether or not genetic testing is accepted [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Pathogenic PSEN1 c.737C>A (p.Ala246Glu); APP and PSEN2 negative
action_criteria.label: Offer an early-onset Alzheimer gene panel only after pre-test genetic counselling; do not use APOE genotype as a diagnostic test
action_criteria.rationale: Onset at 49 with three affected relatives in her mother's generation makes an autosomal-dominant variant likely; testing is the patient's choice after counselling and informs her family more than her own diagnosis [ACMG_NSGC_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Additive QT risk with escitalopram calls for a baseline ECG; ibuprofen adds gastrointestinal risk; no contraindication
action_criteria.label: Check interactions before starting donepezil, given her escitalopram
action_criteria.rationale: Escitalopram and a cholinesterase inhibitor both prolong the QT interval, which changes management (baseline ECG) before treatment starts [NICE_NG97].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal sinus rhythm with a normal QTc
action_criteria.label: Obtain a baseline ECG before starting donepezil with escitalopram
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline QTc is a reasonable pre-treatment safety check when two QT-prolonging drugs are combined; it is not part of the diagnostic work-up [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the decline to anxiety, depression or work stress: objective memory deficits with valid effort, medial temporal atrophy and progression despite escitalopram and CBT are not explained by an affective disorder
Do not order or disclose APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 results without pre-test and post-test genetic counselling
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is indicated for moderate or severe Alzheimer dementia [NICE_NG97]
required_recommendations: Construct a three-generation family pedigree; the affected relatives span two generations (her mother, maternal uncle and maternal aunt, then the patient), an autosomal-dominant pattern
Offer genetic testing only with pre-test and post-test genetic counselling; the result informs the family and not the patient's diagnosis [ACMG_NSGC_2011].

Do not offer predictive testing to the patient's children aged 14 and 17; offer age-appropriate counselling for the family and predictive testing only to adults who request it after counselling [ACMG_NSGC_2011].
Disclose the diagnosis and any genetic result in a planned session with her husband and a genetic counsellor, with follow-up support; respect her brother's decision not to be tested

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines, and a baseline ECG because of escitalopram [NICE_NG97].

Assess driving safety formally and advise on stopping driving until assessed; support her medical leave and a work capability or ill-health retirement process; plan finances, durable power of attorney and advance directives
Offer referral to a dominantly inherited Alzheimer research network or trial registry (for example DIAN) and to young-onset dementia support services for her and her family

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is not part of the dementia work-up; she has no seizures, myoclonus, fluctuation or rapid course
Echocardiography has no role here; she has no cardiac history and no embolic event
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; she has no syncope, palpitations or arrhythmia
Head CT adds nothing when MRI with volumetric sequences is available

accepted: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease with an autosomal-dominant family history

differential.diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) or FTD with genetic cause (GRN, MAPT, C9orf72)
differential.key_features: Young onset and a maternal uncle with personality change raise FTD; against it: an amnestic presentation without disinhibition or apathy, medial temporal and parietal atrophy, Alzheimer biomarkers and a pathogenic PSEN1 variant

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder (depression, anxiety disorder with cognitive complaints)
differential.key_features: Prior attribution to anxiety and depression; against it: progression despite escitalopram and 12 sessions of CBT, valid effort with severe objective memory impairment, MTA 2 atrophy at 51 and a borderline mood score only
Same phenotype and biomarkers; the autosomal-dominant pedigree and the pathogenic PSEN1 variant establish a familial cause

differential.diagnosis: Autoimmune or limbic encephalitis (anti-NMDAR, anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2)
differential.key_features: Two-year gradual course without seizures, encephalopathy or psychiatric break; normal CSF cell count and protein and no mesial temporal signal change

differential.diagnosis: Other genetic dementia (CADASIL, prion disease, mitochondrial)
differential.key_features: No white matter disease for CADASIL, no rapid course or myoclonus for prion disease, no systemic features of mitochondrial disease; the PSEN1 variant explains the disease

key_clinical_evidence: Memory onset at 49 with early-onset dementia in her mother (51), maternal uncle (49) and maternal aunt (53) is an autosomal-dominant pattern across two generations; 'too young for Alzheimer disease' is a common cause of diagnostic delay
PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of dominantly inherited Alzheimer disease, with near-complete penetrance and onset that tends to recur at a similar age within a family [Bateman_2012]

One conclusive biomarker test (CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau, or amyloid PET) is enough to support Alzheimer pathology; the clinical diagnosis does not depend on accepting genetic testing [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET]
Genetic testing requires pre-test and post-test counselling; her children have a 50% a priori risk, and predictive testing is offered only to adults who request it after counselling [ACMG_NSGC_2011]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Objective memory deficits with valid effort, medial temporal atrophy and Alzheimer biomarkers are incompatible with a purely psychiatric explanation; young age does not preclude autosomal-dominant Alzheimer disease
red_herrings.data_point: Age 51 with anxiety and depression attributed to work stress and family history fears; two prior clinicians attributed symptoms to primary psychiatric causes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor cognitive symptoms to anxiety or depression, viewing 51 as too young for AD and attributing the amnestic complaints to affective disorder or medication side effect
red_herrings.location: History of present illness / past medical history

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: An autosomal-dominant pattern of early-onset dementia is the strongest prior indicator of an APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2 variant and warrants offering genetic counselling and testing; the family history is evidence, not only a source of anxiety
red_herrings.data_point: Early-onset dementia in her mother (onset 51), maternal uncle (onset 49) and maternal aunt (onset 53): affected relatives in two generations, the mother's and the patient's
red_herrings.intended_effect: May paradoxically cause an agent to over-anchor on psychiatric causes ('she is anxious because of her family history') rather than recognizing the pedigree as diagnostic evidence mandating genetic testing

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or elevated intracranial pressure, especially relevant in early-onset presentations where mass lesion must be excluded
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.
Genetic testing follows the clinical diagnosis and pre-test counselling.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Young age and prior psychiatric attribution anchor away from AD; the autosomal-dominant pedigree must trigger counselling and an offer of optional testing without making the clinical diagnosis depend on test acceptance
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, brain MRI, and the donepezil interaction check (escitalopram). Optional: one amyloid biomarker test (CSF or amyloid PET), counselled APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 testing, and a baseline ECG before treatment.
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of early-onset AD with an autosomal-dominant pedigree, optional counselled genetic testing, and non-duplicative biomarker use
key_educational_points: Young onset with an autosomal-dominant pedigree warrants offering APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 testing after counselling; testing remains optional
PSEN1 mutations are the most common cause of dominantly inherited AD and carry near-complete penetrance with onset typically in the 40s to 50s
The 'too young for Alzheimer's' heuristic is a documented source of diagnostic delay in familial AD cases

Pre-test and post-test genetic counseling is an ethical obligation before and after disclosure of pathogenic PSEN1 results; predictive testing of children is deferred until they are adults who request it
Decreased CSF Abeta42/40 with raised p-tau supports the biological diagnosis of AD independently of age of onset or genetic status
Genetic testing is optional and requires pre-test counselling; APOE is not used to diagnose Alzheimer disease
Escitalopram with a cholinesterase inhibitor is an additive QT risk: a baseline ECG is a treatment-safety step, not part of the diagnostic work-up

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Eleanor Hartmann is a 51-year-old right-handed high school mathematics teacher who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic, accompanied by her husband, for evaluation of progressive cognitive difficulties over the past two years. She was referred by her primary care physician after multiple workplace concerns led to her being placed on medical leave three months ago.

Her husband first noted subtle changes approximately two years ago: she began misplacing her keys and phone daily, a marked change from her previously meticulous habits. Over the following year, she started making uncharacteristic arithmetic errors — most notably, entering incorrect scores on student grade sheets three times in a single semester, prompting concern from the department chair. She began relying on written notes for tasks she had previously managed entirely from memory, including simple weekly grocery lists and appointment reminders. Her husband describes two episodes in which she drove to the supermarket and, on arriving, could not recall what she had gone to buy, turning around without purchasing anything.

Over the past eight months, symptoms have worsened. She now frequently forgets conversations from earlier in the day, repeating the same questions to her husband within hours. She has difficulty recalling the names of students she has taught for a full semester. She missed three scheduled parent-teacher conferences despite written reminders on her desk; on two occasions, parents waited outside her classroom while she sat unaware inside. The school principal placed her on medical leave citing safety concerns related to students.

Of note, she has a strong and striking family history: her mother developed cognitive symptoms at age 51 (the patient's current age), was formally diagnosed with dementia at 54, required full-time care by 57, and died at 60. Her mother's brother developed cognitive decline at 49 and died in a care facility at 58. Her mother's sister is currently in memory care having noticed memory problems at 53. This pattern of early-onset dementia in two generations on the maternal side has caused extreme distress to the patient and her husband, who present with considerable anxiety about the implications.

She was evaluated by her primary care physician 14 months ago, who attributed her symptoms to anxiety and increased her escitalopram from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. Her mood improved modestly, but the cognitive symptoms did not, and have continued to progress. A psychiatrist she saw 8 months ago considered depression related to work stress and family history anxiety, and recommended cognitive behavioral therapy. She has completed 12 sessions of CBT with no cognitive improvement.

She explicitly acknowledges awareness of her family history and expresses her belief, shared by her husband, that she may have 'the same thing my mother had.' Both ask about genetic testing at the time of the visit. She denies hallucinations, personality change, disinhibition, language difficulty, gait problems, tremor, falls, or bladder dysfunction. No seizures. Sleep is mildly fragmented due to anxiety but no REM behavior disorder is reported.

Luria hand-sequence: learned after 4 repetitions (mildly slowed). No alien limb phenomenon. No anosmia on bedside testing.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements full, no nystagmus or diplopia. Visual fields full to confrontation in all quadrants. Facial sensation and strength symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline, no fasciculations. Fundoscopy: no papilledema.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base, arm swing, and stride length. Tandem gait intact without truncal sway. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and year; gives the correct month but is off by 4 days on date. MoCA 20/30 — loses points on delayed recall (1/5 words spontaneously, 2/5 with category cue), visuospatial/executive (4/5: cube copy imprecise), verbal fluency (8 F-words in 60 seconds), attention (serial subtraction errors), and abstraction (0/2). MMSE 25/30 — loses points on recall (1/3 words at 5 minutes, 1 additional with category cue), one point on orientation (date) and two points on serial sevens (two errors). Conversational speech is fluent and grammatical. Word-finding pauses noted on confrontation naming ('it's the... the number device' for 'calculator'). Digit span forward 6, backward 4. She endorses subjective difficulty 'keeping numbers in mind' and describes frustration that she makes small errors when calculating grades that she would have never made previously.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout, no rigidity or cogwheeling. Strength 5/5 in all extremities bilaterally. No pronator drift. No tremor, myoclonus, or involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No frontal release signs. No Hoffman's sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and vibration sense intact in all extremities. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally. No cortical sensory deficits.
